This Bugatti Tourbillon Miniature Takes 300 Hours To Build and Costs 2027 Honda Civic Money
24 photos
Photo: Amalgam Collection
Spending $24,095 on a car in the United States of America gets you a base compact sedan. Amalgam Collection has a rather different interpretation of what that kind of money should buy, with the British specialist asking this much for each of its 1:8 scale Bugatti Tourbillon replicas. The miniature hypercars measure over 58 centimeters (23 inches) in length and feature the finest quality materials.
Each unit requires over 300 hours of assembly, and its dimensions alone mean that prospective customers might need to rearrange furniture in order to find somewhere suitable to display it. As of this writing, two versions of the scale model reproduce different factory specs of the V16 plug-in hybrid thriller.
Signature Specification leads the way, boasting the launch car's two-tone finish that combines Aerolithe and Aventurine. Only 199 units are in the offing. Equipe Pur Sang Specification is the other one, swapping the understated combo from earlier for Grigio paintwork and Italian Red accents. The Pur Sang recreates the actual vehicle Bugatti used to present said package back in March 2025.
Think of the Pur Sang as the most sporting Tourbillon available for the time being, although 'available' may not be the right word because every single Tourbillon has been spoken for. Additional design elements include a specific front splitter and a more audacious exhaust setup. This one is also limited to 199 examples.
All told, development work required more than 3,000 hours. Amalgam Collection offers bespoke commissions for customers who want their 1:8 scale models to match a particular specification, which means that Amalgam is actually targeting Tourbillon clients rather than average Joes and Janes with deep pockets.
Photo: Amalgam Collection The peeps at Amalgam tasked a small team of craftspeople to put together thousands of individual components, including castings, CNC-machined metal parts, and photo-etched details. More interestingly, the reference material comes from Bugatti's very own material specifications, paint codes, and computer-aided design files. The automaker's own designers and engineers helped Amalgam come up with both designs, ensuring complete accuracy of representation.
An unusually involved development process when you think about it, but hey, both Amalgam and Bugatti understand that attention to detail matters a lot. At this price, which is nearly enough to get you a brand-new Civic sedan for model year 2027, getting anything wrong would be a fairly expensive embarrassment.
On the road, the actual Tourbillon is the first-ever Bug developed with Mate Rimac at the helm. Capable of 1,800 ps (1,775 hp) at full chatter, the Chiron's replacement combines a naturally aspirated V16 developed and produced by Cosworth with no fewer than three electric drive units. Croatian electric hypercar specialist is credited with developing the high-voltage battery and the e-axles, along with the silicon-carbide inverters and torque-vectoring control software.
Tipping the scales at under two metric tons, Bugatti's newest design will be produced in 250 units. Built around a carbon-composite monocoque that integrates the plug-in hybrid battery as a structural element, this bad boy further boasts 3D-printed suspension components and e-actuated dihedral doors.
Flaunting an unashamedly mechanical instrument cluster mounted to a fixed-hub steering wheel, the Tourbillon also features an infotainment screen that can be hidden to clean up the dash. In optimal conditions, the Speed Key enables an electronically limited maximum speed of 276 miles per hour (445 kilometers per hour), making it faster than most Chirons. Only an unrestricted Super Sport 300+ can do better, namely 305 mph (490 kph) in controlled testing conditions.
Via // Amalgam Collection
